p: Paul's letters say Silvanus, the Roman form of the name; Acts calls the same man Silas.
b: Silvanus is the Latin form of the name that Acts writes as Silas. Acts makes him one of the leading men of the Jerusalem church, sent to Antioch with the council's letter (Acts 15:22), then Paul's partner on the journey that brought them to Thessalonica (Acts 15:40; Acts 17:4). Paul names him again as one of the three who preached at Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:19), and 1 Peter 5:12 names a Silvanus as that letter's bearer or scribe. Most readers take all of these to be one man (see the topic page on Silas). Here he stands with Paul and Timothy as a co-sender, so the whole letter speaks as "we." Paul breaks into "I" only at 2:18, 3:5 and 5:27.
r: Acts 15:22; Acts 15:40; Acts 17:4; Acts 17:10; 2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Peter 5:12; 2 Thessalonians 1:1

p: Timothy joined Paul at Lystra and later carried this church's news back to him (3:2, 6).
b: Acts says Timothy was a disciple at Lystra, "His mother was a Jewish believer, and his father a Greek" (Acts 16:1). He traveled with Paul and Silas into Macedonia. In this letter he is the go-between: Paul sends him back to Thessalonica from Athens (3:1-2), and his good report is what sets Paul writing (3:6). Six of Paul's letters name Timothy as a co-sender, which shows how closely the two worked.
r: Acts 16:1-3; Acts 17:14-15; Acts 18:5; 1 Thessalonians 3:2; 1 Thessalonians 3:6; 2 Corinthians 1:1; Philippians 1:1

t: An assembly in a city with its own assembly
p: Ekklesia was the everyday word for a Greek city's assembly of citizens.
b: The Greek ekklesia means a gathering of people called together. In a Greek city it named the citizens' assembly that voted on public business; Acts 19:32-41 uses the word for the town meeting at Ephesus. The Greek Old Testament also uses it for Israel gathered before God. Thessalonica was a free city with its own civic bodies, so a small group of converts who met in a house and called themselves the ekklesia "in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" were using a public word for a new kind of gathering. The phrase "in God the Father" says where this assembly belongs.

p: Paul turns the usual Greek greeting into "grace" and joins it to the Hebrew greeting "peace."
b: A Greek letter usually began "So-and-so to so-and-so, greetings" (chairein, as in Acts 15:23). Paul changes chairein to the similar-sounding charis, "grace," God's kindness that no one earned, and adds "peace," the Greek for the Hebrew greeting shalom. This is the shortest form of the greeting in Paul's letters: the Greek text used here has no "from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (see the variant).
orig: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη (charis hymin kai eirene)

a: the work your faith does, the toil your love takes on
p: Paul's favorite triad appears here, in what may be his first surviving letter, and again at 5:8.
b: Faith, love and hope come as a set here and again in 5:8 ("the breastplate of faith and love, and let the hope of salvation be our helmet"). The best-known form is 1 Corinthians 13:13: "But now these three last: faith, hope and love." Here each virtue is tied to something it does: faith works, love toils, hope endures. The Greek is three short chains of nouns ("the work of the faith," "the labor of the love," "the endurance of the hope"), which the Plain spells out so the reader sees that Paul praises what the virtues produce, not the virtues in the abstract.

p: Hypomone is the staying power that holds up under pressure, which the KJV called "patience."
b: The KJV's "patience of hope" can sound like waiting quietly. The Greek hypomone, literally "remaining under," is the strength to stay put under a load, as in Romans 5:3-4 ("trouble builds endurance"). The Thessalonians were under real pressure (1:6; 2:14; 3:3-4), and their hope in the Lord's coming (1:10) is what kept them standing.

p: The Greek plural adelphoi, "brothers," was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women.
b: The word "brother" or "brothers" comes nineteen times in this short letter, most often as Paul's way of addressing the readers. The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way to address a group that included women, as Acts 1:15-16 and Romans 16 show, so many recent Bibles write "brothers and sisters." This site keeps "brothers," as in Acts and Romans, with that gloss. The word matters here: converts who had lost family and friends by leaving their gods (1:9; 2:14) were given a new family, with Paul as their nurse and father (2:7, 11) and one another as brothers (4:9-10).

p: Paul uses Israel's word for God's choosing, eklogē, of a church of former idol worshipers.
b: The Greek is "knowing ... your election." In the Bible God's choosing is first Israel's privilege: "The LORD your God has chosen you" (Deuteronomy 7:6). Paul applies it to Gentiles who had worshiped idols until a few months before (1:9), and he bases it on what he saw: the message came with power and the Spirit (1:5), and they received it with joy in hard times (1:6). How God's choosing relates to human response is debated between traditions (see the topic page); this verse simply treats it as known from its effects.

p: Euangelion means good news, a message announced; English Bibles usually say "gospel."
b: The Greek euangelion ("good news") is the word behind the Old English "gospel" ("good tale"). The Greek Old Testament uses the related verb for the herald who runs with news of victory (Isaiah 52:7). Paul says "our good news" because it is the message he and his partners carried, not because it was theirs. The noun comes six times in this short letter (1:5; 2:2, 4, 8, 9; 3:2), always as something spoken aloud and received.

a: with power too, and with the Holy Spirit
p: Paul may mean miracles, or the force with which the message took hold, or both.
b: Paul says the message did not come "in words only." Some readers take "power" as signs and miracles, since Paul elsewhere speaks of his preaching "with the power of signs and wonders, and with the power of the Spirit of God" (Romans 15:19; compare 1 Corinthians 2:4). Others read it as the inner force with which the message gripped both preachers and hearers, since the next phrase is "great certainty" and the verse goes on to the preachers' own conduct. Many commentators hold both together. The letter's own evidence is the converts' changed life (1:9-10).

p: Acts tells of a riot, a raid on Jason's house and a hurried escape by night.
b: Acts 17:5-10 describes how the church began in uproar: a crowd gathered, Jason's house was stormed, Jason and "some of the brothers" were hauled before the city rulers, and Paul and Silas were sent off "That same night" (Acts 17:10). The charge was that "They all break Caesar's decrees by saying that Jesus is another king" (Acts 17:7). The letter speaks of the same pressure: "trouble" (thlipsis) here, suffering from their own countrymen (2:14), and troubles that Paul had warned would come (3:3-4).

p: Macedonia in the north and Achaia in the south made up Roman Greece; Thessalonica was Macedonia's capital.
b: Rome divided Greece into two provinces: Macedonia, with Thessalonica as its capital from 128 BC, and Achaia, with Corinth as its seat. Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, the first three churches Paul founded in Europe (Acts 16-17), were in Macedonia; Athens and Corinth were in Achaia. Saying that the Thessalonians were a pattern for believers in both provinces means, in effect, all the Christians in Greece. Paul was probably in Corinth, in Achaia, when he wrote.

p: The verb is used of a sound that echoes outward, like a trumpet blast or thunder.
b: Execheo is the root of English "echo": a sound that rings out and carries. Thessalonica sat on the Via Egnatia, the Roman road that ran across the Balkans from the Adriatic coast to Byzantium, and was a port as well, so news from the city traveled fast. Paul's "every place" is a happy exaggeration, but travelers along those roads and sea lanes could have carried word of a whole group of Gentiles who had given up their gods.

a: turned away from idols to God
p: The letter speaks to former idol worshipers, while Acts tells mostly of synagogue converts.
b: "Turning" from idols to the living God is the language of Jewish teaching to Gentiles and of the prophets' call to Israel. The phrase shows that most of the first readers were Gentiles who had worshiped the city's gods. Acts 17:2-4 says Paul argued in the synagogue for three Sabbaths and won over some Jews, "a large number of Greeks who worshiped God, and many women of the first rank." Readers explain the difference in several ways: Acts tells only the start, and Paul stayed longer than three weeks (Philippians 4:16 says gifts reached him there more than once); or the letter's readers were mostly Gentiles converted outside the synagogue; or Luke shaped his account to fit his pattern of beginning with the synagogue.
r: Acts 17:2-4; Acts 14:15; Acts 15:19; 1 Corinthians 12:2; Galatians 4:8-9; Philippians 4:16

a: a God who lives and is true
p: A Jewish way of naming the one God against idols that are lifeless and false.
b: Jeremiah sets the LORD against the idols in the same terms: "But the LORD is God in truth. / He himself is the living God and a king who lasts forever" (Jeremiah 10:10). Idols are made by hands, cannot speak and cannot save; the true God lives and acts. The Greek here has no "the": "to serve God living and true," which the Plain gives as "a God who lives and is true" so the description stands out. To "serve" (douleuo) is literally to work as a slave for him.

a: to wait for his Son to come from the heavens
t: The first preaching in a nutshell?
p: Verses 9-10 may summarize what missionaries taught Gentiles: one God, his Son, the resurrection, the coming judgment.
b: Many scholars think 1:9-10 sums up the early preaching to Gentiles, perhaps in a set form Paul used: turn from idols to the one God, wait for his Son from heaven, whom God raised, who rescues from the coming anger. Paul's speech to the Athenians in Acts has the same outline (one God, judgment, a man raised from the dead: Acts 17:31). Others see Paul's own wording and doubt a fixed formula. Either way, the verse puts the hope of Christ's coming at the heart of what new believers learned first, which explains why his coming fills this letter (2:19; 3:13; 4:13-5:11; 5:23).

p: Orge, God's anger ("wrath"), here is the judgment of the last day.
b: The Greek orge is "anger"; English Bibles often say "wrath." It is God's settled opposition to evil, which the prophets expected on "the day of the LORD" (Amos 5:18; Zephaniah 1:15). Paul uses the word three times in this letter: the anger that is coming (here), the anger that "has reached" Paul's opponents (2:16), and the anger God did not appoint believers to face (5:9). Jesus "rescues" (present tense) from it now, not only at the end.
r: Romans 5:9; Romans 1:18; Amos 5:18; Zephaniah 1:15; 1 Thessalonians 2:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:9

p: This "coming" is eisodos, Paul's arrival in town, not the parousia of 2:19.
b: English uses "coming" for two Greek words in this letter. Here eisodos means "entrance" or "visit" (as in 1:9, "the kind of welcome we had"). In 2:19, 3:13, 4:15 and 5:23 the word is parousia, the Lord's coming. Paul's point is that his visit was not "empty" (kene): it produced a church.

p: Just before Thessalonica, Paul and Silas had been stripped, beaten and jailed at Philippi.
b: Acts 16:19-24 tells the story: "The magistrates ripped the clothes off them and gave the order to beat them with rods" (Acts 16:22). Paul later protested that they were Roman citizens who had been flogged in public without a trial (Acts 16:37). The word Paul uses here, "treated with insults" (hybristhentes), is a word for public shame. Philippi lies east of Thessalonica on the same Roman road, the Via Egnatia, so the Thessalonians could easily have heard the story.

p: Parresiazomai is the citizen's right to speak openly, here used with the courage it takes.
b: In Greek cities parresia was the free citizen's right to speak his mind in the assembly. In Acts the word describes the apostles speaking openly under threat (Acts 4:13, 29, 31). Paul joins it to courage: after Philippi he could have kept quiet, but "relying on our God" he spoke as freely as before.

a: there is no trickery in it
p: Greek cities knew wandering speakers who taught for money or fame; Paul says he is not one of them.
b: Verses 3-12 read like a defense. The Greek world had many traveling teachers and speakers, philosophers and preachers of new gods, and many people suspected them of flattery, greed and trickery. Paul denies each charge: no error, no impurity, no tricks (2:3), no flattery or greed (2:5), no hunt for praise (2:6), no burden on anyone (2:9). Scholars debate whether real critics in Thessalonica were saying this, or whether Paul is using a common way of describing a true teacher against a false one so the church can see the difference. Either way, the converts were being told that the men who had fled town were frauds.

a: who puts our hearts to the test
p: The prophets and Psalms speak of God testing the heart, the hidden center of a person.
b: "You test the kidneys and the heart" (Jeremiah 11:20). Paul uses the same verb, dokimazo, twice in this verse: God tested and approved the preachers, and God keeps testing their hearts. The verb is used of testing metal to see if it is genuine. Paul's appeal is that the Thessalonians can trust a message whose bearers answer to that kind of examiner.

p: Paul includes Silvanus and Timothy as "apostles," a wider use than the Twelve.
b: The plural takes in all three senders. An apostolos is someone sent with a commission. Paul uses the word for himself and for others beyond the Twelve, such as Andronicus and Junia, "outstanding among the apostles" (Romans 16:7), and the messengers of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23). Here the title explains the right they did not use: to be supported by those they served.

p: En barei, "in weight," can mean making demands for support, or standing on one's rank.
b: The Greek says the apostles "could be in weight." The word means weight or burden, and also importance or dignity. Paul may mean that they could have asked to be supported, a burden on the church (as 2:9 uses a related verb, "be a weight on"), or that they could have stood on their authority as Christ's apostles. The Plain keeps the double sense. (In the Greek editions this phrase is the first part of verse 7.)

p: Paul piles up family images: infants (or gentle), a nurse, a father (2:11), an orphan (2:17).
b: A trophos was a woman who nursed and raised children, often a hired wet nurse or a household slave; here she cares for "her own children," which makes the warmth stronger. If the first word of the verse is "infants" (see the variant), Paul has jumped from one picture to the next: he became like a baby among them (without guile, without demands), then like a nurse warming her children, then like a father urging them on (2:11-12), then like an orphan torn from them (2:17). The images clash, but each makes the same point about the bond between preachers and converts.

p: Paul supported himself with his hands; Acts says his trade was making tents.
b: Acts says of Paul at Corinth: "Their craft was making tents" (Acts 18:3). Work with leather or tent cloth could be done in a shop where people stopped to talk, so the workshop may have been one of the places he taught. Paul says he worked "so we would not be a weight on any of you," though he did accept gifts from the church at Philippi while he was in Thessalonica (Philippians 4:16). His example becomes a lesson in 4:11 and in 2 Thessalonians 3:7-9.
r: Acts 18:3; Acts 20:34; 1 Corinthians 4:12; 2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:16; 2 Thessalonians 3:7-9

p: Paul's word for a whole way of life is "walk," from the Hebrew idiom.
b: The Greek peripateo means to walk around. Paul uses it, as the Hebrew Bible uses halak, for how a person lives. Later Jewish teaching called the path of practice halakhah, "the walking." This letter uses the verb for the whole moral teaching of chapter 4 (4:1, 12). The Plain keeps "walk" so the reader can follow the thread.

p: One of the few places Paul speaks of God's kingdom, here as something believers are being called into.
b: "Kingdom" (basileia) means God's reign as king. The Gospels make it the center of Jesus' preaching; Paul names it less often, usually as a future inheritance (1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Galatians 5:21). Here the present participle says God "is calling" them into it now. In a city where Paul's preaching of "another king" had caused a riot (Acts 17:7), the word had a political edge.

a: it is at work in you who believe
p: God's word is not only heard; it goes on acting (energeitai) in those who believe.
b: The verb energeo (behind English "energy") is used of a power at work. The Thessalonians took the preachers' message as God's own word, and that word kept working in them: in their faith, love and endurance (1:3) and in their standing firm under pressure (2:14). The prophets speak of God's word as active: "Is my word not like fire, the LORD declares" (Jeremiah 23:29).

a: God's churches that are in Judea
p: The first Jewish believers in Judea suffered from their neighbors, as the Thessalonians now did.
b: Paul knew the Judean churches had been persecuted; he had done some of it himself (Galatians 1:13, 22-23). Acts tells of the persecution after Stephen, when "the church in Jerusalem came under severe persecution" (Acts 8:1), and of King Herod Agrippa I, who killed James (Acts 12:1-3). Paul's comparison is between two churches persecuted by their own people: Gentile believers by Gentile neighbors in Thessalonica, Jewish believers by Jewish neighbors in Judea.

p: Paul blames their own countrymen; Acts says the Jews of Thessalonica stirred up the trouble.
b: The Greek symphyletes means someone of the same tribe or people. Since the readers were mostly Gentiles (1:9), their "own countrymen" were Gentile neighbors. Acts 17:5-9 puts the blame on "The Jews" of Thessalonica, who "recruited some low men who loitered in the marketplace." The two accounts can fit together: Acts tells how the trouble began, and the letter tells what the converts were still facing months later from families and neighbors. Some readers think the word could include local Jews as fellow citizens of the city.

p: In context hoi Ioudaioi means the Judeans who persecuted the churches in Judea; a comma decides how far the words reach.
b: The Greek Ioudaioi can mean Jews in general or people of Judea, "Judeans." Here Paul is speaking of those who persecuted the churches "in Judea." Paul himself was a Jew, as were the Judean believers he praises. The Greek manuscripts have no punctuation. Most editions and translations put a comma after "the Jews," which makes 2:15-16 describe Jews in general. Frank Gilliard (New Testament Studies, 1989) argued that the clause should be read without the comma, as a limiting description: "the Jews who killed the Lord Jesus," that is, the particular Judeans responsible. The Plain keeps the usual comma, as the Greek allows both, and the deep dive on this chapter gives the case for each.
orig: τῶν Ἰουδαίων (ton Ioudaion), 'the Jews / the Judeans'

p: Jesus was crucified by a Roman governor; Paul blames Judean opponents; later Christians made this a charge against all Jews.
b: Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, and the Gospels say Pilate gave the order. They also give a role to the temple leaders and a crowd in Jerusalem. Paul's sentence is a sharp polemic within a Jewish quarrel, written by a Jew about the Judean opponents of the Judean churches. Later Christians read verses like this, and Matthew 27:25 ("His blood on us, and on our children!"), as a charge of "deicide" against all Jews of every age, and it fed centuries of contempt and violence. The Catholic Church's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) says that what happened in Christ's passion "cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today," and other churches have made similar statements.

p: A charge Israel's own Scriptures make against Israel, which Jesus repeats.
b: The charge comes from inside the Jewish Scriptures. Elijah complains, "They have killed your prophets with the sword" (1 Kings 19:10), and the prayer of Nehemiah 9:26 confesses that Israel's ancestors killed the prophets God sent. Jesus says the same to the scribes and Pharisees: "you are the sons of the men who murdered the prophets" (Matthew 23:31; compare Luke 11:49-50). Paul is using a theme of Jewish self-criticism. The Byzantine text and the KJV read "their own prophets" (see the variant).
r: 1 Kings 19:10; Nehemiah 9:26; Jeremiah 26:20-23; Matthew 23:31; Luke 11:49-50; Acts 7:52

a: they set themselves against all people
t: A charge also made by pagans
p: Greek and Roman writers accused Jews of hostility to outsiders; Paul's words sound like that slur.
b: Some Greek and Roman writers said that Jews kept apart from and despised other peoples. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing some fifty years after Paul, says they "regard the rest of mankind with all the hatred of enemies" (Histories 5.5, in the Church and Brodribb translation). Paul's phrase sounds like this slur, and this is one reason some scholars think the verses were added by a later, non-Jewish hand (see the chapter page). Others note that Paul explains himself in the next verse: the hostility he means is the effort to stop the good news from reaching Gentiles.

p: Eis to with an infinitive can give a result or a purpose; the Plain takes it as the result, with most English versions.
b: The Greek says eis to anaplerosai, literally "so as to fill up," with pantote, "always." This construction can state a result (what their actions lead to) or a purpose (what they were aiming at). SIL's Translator's Notes on this verse list the BSB, the NIV, the NRSV, the NET Bible and several others for the result reading, and the KJV, the RSV and the Jerusalem Bible for the purpose reading, and they recommend the result reading with the majority of English versions. The Plain follows that choice. Read as purpose, the clause is harsher: it would say that the persecutors were set on sinning to the full. Either way the picture of a measure filled to the top comes from the Scriptures (see the next note).
orig: εἰς τὸ ἀναπληρῶσαι αὐτῶν τὰς ἁμαρτίας πάντοτε (eis to anaplerosai auton tas hamartias pantote)

a: fill up the measure of their sins
p: An old biblical picture: sin piles up until it reaches the full measure and judgment falls.
b: God tells Abraham that his descendants must wait, "for the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16). Jesus says to his opponents, "You, then, fill up your fathers' measure!" (Matthew 23:32). Jewish writings of the period use the same picture of a measure of sin that, once full, brings judgment. Paul uses it of those who block the good news.

a: the anger has reached them in the end
t: "In the end": what anger, and when?
p: Eis telos can mean "at last," "fully" or "until the end"; the past tense has puzzled readers.
b: Two parts of this line are debated. Eis telos can mean "at last," "completely" or "to the end" (that is, for good). And the verb ephthasen is past: the anger "has reached" or "has come upon" them. Readers offer three main explanations: Paul means some disaster of the 40s that he saw as a sign of judgment; he speaks of the coming judgment as already certain, as the prophets often used the past tense of what God will do; or the verse looks back on the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, which would mean a later writer added it (see the chapter page). Romans 11 shows Paul's fuller and very different word about Israel: "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26).

p: Aporphanizo means to be made an orphan; Paul, who called himself their nurse and father, now feels like a bereaved child.
b: The verb is built on orphanos, "orphan," and could be used of a parent losing children as well as children losing parents. Paul turns his family picture around once more (2:7, 11): the departure from Thessalonica, forced and sudden (Acts 17:10), left him feeling bereaved.

p: Paul does not say; guesses include Jason's bond, illness, and continued opposition.
b: The verb enkopto means to cut into a road, to block it. Paul sees Satan behind whatever kept him away, but does not name it. Some think of the bond the city officials made Jason post (Acts 17:9), which may have depended on Paul's staying away; others think of Paul's illness (2 Corinthians 12:7), or the Jews from Thessalonica who followed him to Berea (Acts 17:13). In Romans 1:13 Paul says only that "something has stopped me." The letter shows a writer who saw unseen powers in ordinary setbacks, without letting that excuse the setbacks.

t: A wreath, not a king's crown
p: Stephanos was the wreath given to winners of games and honored citizens.
b: A stephanos was a wreath of leaves, given to an athlete who won, or to a citizen the city wished to honor. It is not usually a royal crown. Paul pictures himself on the day of Christ's coming holding up the church as his prize (compare Philippians 4:1, where Paul calls the Philippians his joy and his wreath).

p: Parousia meant arrival or presence, and was used of a ruler's visit; here it is the Lord's return.
b: Parousia means "presence" or "arrival." In Greek it could mean any arrival, but it was also used of a ruler's official visit to a city. Adolf Deissmann drew attention to this use in papyri and inscriptions. This letter is the first in the New Testament to use the word for Jesus' coming (2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23); Matthew 24 and 1 Corinthians 15:23 use it too. The word does not by itself say "second" or "return": it is the arrival of the Lord in person.
r: 1 Thessalonians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 4:15; 1 Thessalonians 5:23; Matthew 24:3; 1 Corinthians 15:23; 2 Thessalonians 2:1

p: The letter has Timothy with Paul in Athens; Acts has him join Paul only at Corinth.
b: Acts says Silas and Timothy stayed in Berea when Paul went on to Athens (Acts 17:14-15), and that they joined him later at Corinth: "Once Silas and Timothy had come down from Macedonia" (Acts 18:5). The letter says Paul sent Timothy back to Thessalonica from Athens. The usual way to fit them together is that Timothy came to Athens as Paul asked (Acts 17:15), was sent back north, and then met Paul again at Corinth with his report (3:6). Others think Acts has simplified the movements, and they give the letter, as the earlier and first-hand source, the better claim. Paul repeats the point in 3:5 with "I."

a: this is the lot we were given
p: Keimetha means "we are laid down for" this: suffering is part of the calling, not a sign that something went wrong.
b: The verb keimai means "lie" or "be set," and here "be appointed." New converts might think that their troubles proved the message false or God absent. Paul says he had told them in advance (3:4) that believers are set down for this. Acts gives the same teaching: "We must go through many troubles to enter the kingdom of God" (Acts 14:22). The same idea of being appointed returns in 5:9, where God has not appointed them to face anger.

p: Ho peirazon, "the one who tests," is Satan, the name Matthew uses at Jesus' testing in the wilderness.
b: The Greek verb peirazo means both "test" and "tempt." Matthew uses the same participle as a name for Satan: "The tester came up to him" (Matthew 4:3). Paul fears that pressure from outside (3:3-4) might have been used by Satan, already named in 2:18, to break their faith, so that his work would "come to nothing," the same empty result he denied in 2:1.
orig: ὁ πειράζων (ho peirazon), 'the one who tests'

a: with the good news of your faith and your love
p: Paul uses the verb for "bring good news" of Timothy's report, a word he usually keeps for the gospel.
b: The verb is euangelizomai, "announce good news," which elsewhere in Paul nearly always means preaching the gospel. Here it is Timothy's report about the church. The choice shows how much the news meant: the church's faith and love were good news to Paul. Notice that hope is missing from the report, though faith, love and hope came together in 1:3. Some readers think that is why the next chapters say so much about hope (4:13-5:11).

p: Paul's own life depends, in a sense, on the church's standing firm.
b: The Greek is short: "because now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord." Paul does not mean that his survival depends on the Thessalonians, but that their faithfulness gives him life and strength in the middle of his own hardship (3:7). The verb steko, "stand firm," is a soldier's word for holding a position.

a: what is still missing in your faith
p: The church's faith was real but young; chapters 4 and 5 may supply some of what was lacking.
b: Paul had been forced to leave after a short stay (2:17), so the converts' teaching was incomplete. The word hysterema means a lack or shortfall. Many readers see chapters 4 and 5 as Paul supplying it by letter: how to live in holiness (4:1-8), how to work (4:11-12), what happens to the dead (4:13-18) and how to wait for the day of the Lord (5:1-11). Others think "faith" here includes their trust under pressure, which only time and presence could strengthen.

a: our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus
p: God and Jesus together are the subject of a prayer whose verb is singular.
b: The verb "open a straight road" (kateuthynai) is singular in Greek, though it has two subjects: God the Father and the Lord Jesus. Grammar alone cannot prove much, since Greek sometimes gives a single verb to a pair. But the prayer itself is striking: in what is probably one of the earliest Christian writings, a Jewish writer prays to the Lord Jesus together with God the Father, and in 3:12 asks "the Lord" alone to make their love grow. Later Christian teaching on the Trinity drew on texts like this one.

t: His holy ones: angels or believers?
p: The words echo Zechariah 14:5, where the holy ones coming with the LORD are angels; Paul may mean believers too.
b: Zechariah 14:5 ends, "And the LORD my God will arrive, and all the holy ones will be with you." In Zechariah the holy ones are God's heavenly army, and Jesus speaks of coming "with his angels" (Matthew 16:27). But Paul usually calls believers hagioi, "the saints," and 4:14 says God will bring the dead believers "with him." So the holy ones may be angels, believers who have died, or both. The Plain says "holy ones," as Zechariah 14:5 and Jude 1:14 do on this site, so that the angels stay possible, rather than "saints," which would decide for believers.
orig: μετὰ πάντων τῶν ἁγίων αὐτοῦ (meta panton ton hagion autou)
r: Zechariah 14:5; Jude 1:14; Matthew 16:27; Matthew 25:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:14; 2 Thessalonians 1:7

p: Paralambano, "take over," is the word for receiving a tradition passed down.
b: The verb paralambano was used for receiving teaching passed on by a teacher. Paul uses it and its partner paradidomi, "hand on," of the most basic Christian teaching: "I handed on to you what I also received" (1 Corinthians 15:3; compare 1 Corinthians 11:23). Here it is the moral teaching he gave in person: how to "walk and please God." The Thessalonians had a body of teaching from the start, before any letter was written; 2 Thessalonians 2:15 names it "the traditions." The traditions debate how this oral teaching relates to Scripture (see the topic page).

p: Parangeliai are commands passed down a line, as from an officer.
b: The word parangelia is used of instructions given with authority, such as orders passed along in an army. "Through the Lord Jesus" means the orders came with his authority, not Paul's own. Paul uses the related verb in 4:11 ("just as we instructed you").

p: Hagiasmos is the process of becoming holy; here it begins with sexual conduct.
b: The noun hagiasmos means making holy or the holiness that results, and comes three times in six verses (4:3, 4, 7). The Torah gives the call: "You will be holy, because I am holy, I the LORD your God" (Leviticus 19:2). For Gentile converts, Paul says, God's will for holiness starts with the body and with sex, the area where Greek city life and Israel's law differed most.

t: Sexual sin in a Greek city
p: Porneia covered all sex outside marriage, which Greek and Roman custom allowed men in many forms.
b: Porneia began as the word for prostitution and by the first century covered sexual sin in general. Greek and Roman custom was often relaxed about men having sex with prostitutes, slaves and others outside marriage. The Jewish law and Jewish teachers rejected all of this, and Paul held the Gentile converts to the same standard. The Jerusalem council's letter to Gentile believers also asked them to "keep away from" sexual sin (Acts 15:29), with the same verb Paul uses here.

p: Skeuos means a jar or tool; here it may mean one's body, one's wife, or (some say) one's sexual organ.
b: Paul says each one should know how to ktasthai his own skeuos. Skeuos is a pot, jar or tool. Ktaomai usually means "acquire" or "get," and some think it can mean "gain control of." Three main readings follow. (1) "Control your own body," as John Chrysostom read it (Homily 5 on 1 Thessalonians): "we possess our vessel, when it is pure"; compare 2 Corinthians 4:7. (2) "Get a wife of your own" in a holy way, rather than using prostitutes, with 1 Peter 3:7 (the wife as the "weaker vessel") and 1 Corinthians 7:2. (3) A polite word for the male sexual organ. The KJV's "possess his vessel" keeps the puzzle. The Plain keeps "vessel" and uses "gain control of" for the verb, which fits the first and third readings best but does not shut out the second.
orig: τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σκεῦος κτᾶσθαι (to heautou skeuos ktasthai)

a: as the Gentiles are, who do not know God
p: Paul speaks to Gentile converts as if they no longer belong among "the Gentiles."
b: Paul writes to people who were born Gentiles, yet he sets them apart from "the Gentiles who do not know God," as Jewish writers set Israel apart from the nations. Leviticus warns Israel against the sexual practices of the peoples of Canaan: "for by all of these the nations that I am driving out ahead of you made themselves unclean" (Leviticus 18:24). Paul does the same with 1 Corinthians 12:2: "when you were Gentiles." Many scholars see in this that Paul thought of his converts as joined to Israel's God, holy like Israel, without becoming Jews.

p: "In this matter" may continue the subject of sex, or turn to cheating in trade.
b: The Greek en to pragmati means "in the matter" or "in the deal," and pragma can mean a business affair. Some readers think Paul turns here from sex to greedy dealing in business. Most think he is still speaking of sex: adultery or seduction "crosses the line" and wrongs another man, a fellow believer, whose wife or household is harmed. The verb pleonekteo, "take more than one's share," fits both.
orig: ὑπερβαίνειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν ... ἐν τῷ πράγματι (hyperbainein kai pleonektein ... en to pragmati)

p: The words echo Psalm 94:1; the "Lord" may be God or Jesus.
b: "God who takes vengeance, LORD, / God who takes vengeance, shine out!" (Psalm 94:1). The Greek ekdikos is a judge or agent who sets wrongs right. Paul's warning puts sexual wrongs among the matters God will judge, even when no court would. In this letter "the Lord" usually means Jesus (1:6; 3:12; 4:15-17), and Paul may mean that Jesus will act as judge at his coming.

p: Paul's words echo Ezekiel's promise that God would put his Spirit within his people.
b: Paul says God gives his Holy Spirit "into" you (eis hymas), which echoes Ezekiel: "I will put my own Spirit inside you. I will cause you to walk by my rules" (Ezekiel 36:27), and "I will place my Spirit in you so that you live" (Ezekiel 37:14). The point is that holiness is not only a rule but God's own Spirit living in them, so rejecting the call to holiness is rejecting God. The critical text has the present tense "gives"; the Textus Receptus has "has given" and "to us" (see the variant).

p: Philadelphia was a word for love between real brothers and sisters; Paul uses it for a church of unrelated people.
b: In Greek writers philadelphia means the love of brothers and sisters for one another in a family. Paul uses it for the love that binds people who are not related at all. In a church where many had been cut off from their own families and neighbors (2:14), being treated as kin by fellow believers was a practical matter: help, hospitality, shared meals.

a: God himself has been your teacher
p: Theodidaktoi, "God-taught," recalls Isaiah 54:13 and Jeremiah 31:34.
b: The single Greek word theodidaktoi means "God-taught." It recalls Isaiah 54:13, "All your children will be the LORD's learners," which John's Gospel quotes as "And all of them will be taught by God" (John 6:45), and the new covenant promise that God's people will no longer need to be told, "Know the LORD!" (Jeremiah 31:34). Paul may mean that the Spirit (4:8) teaches love from within, so that the church needs no letter on the subject.

p: Paul's call to a quiet life and to work may answer idleness, dependence on patrons, or public trouble.
b: Paul asks the church to be ambitious about something unusual: being quiet. Three explanations are common. (1) Some believers had stopped working because they expected the Lord to come soon; 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12 deals with people who would not work, and 5:14 warns those "out of line." (2) Some poorer members were living as clients of richer patrons, or of the church, and Paul wants them to support themselves, as he did (2:9). (3) After the uproar of Acts 17, Paul wants the church to give outsiders no cause for complaint (4:12). These can be combined. "Working with your hands" assumes that many of the readers were manual workers.
r: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:14; Acts 17:5-9; Acts 20:34-35; Ephesians 4:28

p: A new group meeting in houses drew suspicion; their conduct was the church's public face.
b: "Those outside" are non-believers. Small groups that met privately, refused the city's gods and spoke of "another king" (Acts 17:7) were easy to suspect. Paul wants their daily life to answer the suspicion: decent conduct, honest work, and no need to beg. Compare Colossians 4:5 and 1 Corinthians 5:12-13.

p: Koimaomai, "fall asleep," was a common way to speak of death; by itself it does not teach that the soul sleeps.
b: Greeks and Jews both spoke of the dead as sleeping, and the word for a burial place, koimeterion ("cemetery"), comes from the same root. Daniel 12:2 uses the image for the dead who will rise: "Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up." Paul uses it for believers who have died (4:13-15; 1 Corinthians 15:6, 18, 20). The picture suits a death that is not final, since sleepers wake. Whether the dead are conscious until the resurrection is a separate question, on which the churches differ (see the card and the topic page).
r: Daniel 12:2; 1 Corinthians 15:6; 1 Corinthians 15:18; 1 Corinthians 15:20; John 11:11-14; Acts 7:60

p: Either the converts had not been taught about resurrection, or they feared their dead would miss the Lord's coming.
b: Paul does not forbid grief; he forbids grief without hope. Why the Thessalonians lacked hope is debated. Some think Paul's short stay left no time to teach about the resurrection of believers, so they did not know that the dead would rise. Others think they knew of resurrection but feared that those who died before the Lord came would miss the great day, or be at a disadvantage (4:15). Many of their pagan neighbors did not expect the dead to rise in the body, though some philosophers taught the soul's survival.

p: The phrase may belong with "fell asleep" or with "will bring."
b: The Greek runs "those who fell asleep through Jesus God will bring with him." "Through Jesus" may go with "fell asleep" (believers who died in union with Jesus, or even died as martyrs because of him) or with "will bring" (God will bring them by means of Jesus). Both readings say that the dead believers' future depends on Jesus' own death and rising. The Plain keeps the Greek order so that both remain possible.
orig: τοὺς κοιμηθέντας διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ (tous koimethentas dia tou Iesou)

p: Paul may cite a saying of Jesus not in the Gospels, sum up Jesus' teaching, or pass on a prophecy.
b: Paul claims a "word of the Lord" for what follows. Three views are common. (1) A saying of Jesus that the Gospels do not record (scholars call such sayings agrapha). (2) Paul's own summary of Jesus' teaching on his coming, which has many of the same features: the Son of Man coming on the clouds, the trumpet, the gathering of the chosen (Matthew 24:30-31). (3) A message from the risen Lord given through a prophet, perhaps Paul himself. Where Paul has a saying of Jesus elsewhere he says so (1 Corinthians 7:10; 1 Corinthians 11:23).

a: we who are alive, who remain
t: Did Paul expect to be alive?
p: Paul writes "we who are alive"; scholars debate whether he expected to live until the Lord came.
b: Paul counts himself with "we who are alive, who remain." Many scholars think he expected the Lord to come in his own lifetime, and some trace a change in his later letters, where he faces death (2 Corinthians 5:8: "we would much prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord"; Philippians 1:21-23). Others say "we" only means "whichever of us are alive then," and note that Paul refuses to set a date (5:1-2) and speaks in 1 Corinthians 15:51 both ways: "not all of us will sleep." The question of delay is taken up on the topic page.

p: The KJV's "shall not prevent" meant "shall not go before," the older sense of "prevent."
b: The Greek phthano means to arrive first or get ahead of. The KJV's "shall not prevent them which are asleep" used "prevent" in its old sense, from Latin praevenire, "come before." Today it sounds as if the living could stop the dead from rising. Paul's point is about order: the living will have no head start over the dead.
orig: οὐ μὴ φθάσωμεν (ou me phthasomen), 'we will by no means precede'

p: Keleusma is a command given out loud: an officer to troops, a captain to rowers.
b: Keleusma is a shouted order, such as an officer gives to troops or a coxswain to rowers. The verse has three sounds: the shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet. Paul does not say who shouts. Some think it is the Lord himself calling the dead, as Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43) and spoke of an hour "in which everyone lying in the tombs will hear his voice" (John 5:28).

p: The only other archangel named in the Bible is Michael, whom Daniel links to the time of the resurrection.
b: The word archangelos, "chief angel," comes in the Bible only here and in Jude 1:9: "Michael the archangel." Daniel 12:1-2 sets Michael's rising at the time of the great distress, when "Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up." Paul names no angel; the phrase "an archangel's voice" has no article in Greek.

p: A trumpet blast marks God's coming at Sinai and the gathering of his people in the prophets.
b: At Sinai there was "the blast of a ram's horn, extremely loud" (Exodus 19:16). The prophets expected a great horn to gather the scattered people (Isaiah 27:13) and the Lord himself to "blast the ram's horn" (Zechariah 9:14). Jesus speaks of angels sent "with a great trumpet" to gather his chosen (Matthew 24:31), and Paul writes to Corinth: "at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised free of decay, and we ourselves will be changed" (1 Corinthians 15:52).
r: Exodus 19:16; Isaiah 27:13; Zechariah 9:14; Joel 2:1; Matthew 24:31; 1 Corinthians 15:52

a: Those who are dead in Christ will rise first
p: "First" means before the living are caught up, not a first resurrection of believers set apart from a later one.
b: In context, "first" answers the worry of 4:13-15: the dead in Christ rise first, "Next" the living are caught up "along with them" (4:17). Paul is ordering two groups of believers. Some premillennial readers connect the verse with the "first resurrection" of Revelation 20:5-6, a resurrection of believers before the thousand years; amillennial and other readers say Paul says nothing here about the resurrection of unbelievers or a later one.

p: Harpazo means snatch or seize; the Latin rapiemur gave English the word "rapture."
b: The Greek harpazo means to seize suddenly, as a thief or a wild animal does, or to snatch someone away. The New Testament uses it when the Spirit "snatched Philip away" (Acts 8:39), when Paul was "snatched up as far as the third heaven" (2 Corinthians 12:2), and when the woman's child "was snatched up to God and to his throne" (Revelation 12:5). The Latin Vulgate translates this verse rapiemur, "we will be snatched up," and from that Latin verb comes the English word "rapture." The verse names the event; when it happens in relation to other end-time events is the subject of the card on this chapter.

p: Clouds mark God's presence; the Son of Man comes with them and Jesus went up in one.
b: In the Bible clouds are the sign of God's presence: the cloud on Sinai, the cloud over the tabernacle, the one like a son of man "coming with the clouds of heaven" (Daniel 7:13). At the ascension "a cloud received him" (Acts 1:9), and the angels promise that he "will come this same way" (Acts 1:11). Paul's believers are carried up into the same sign of God's presence.

t: Going out to meet a ruler
p: Apantesis was used of a city going out to greet an arriving dignitary; whether Paul meant that picture is debated.
b: The phrase is eis apantesin, "for a meeting." When an emperor or governor visited a city, leading citizens went out to meet him and escort him in. John Chrysostom already read the verse this way: "For when a king drives into a city, those who are in honor go out to meet him" (Homily 8 on 1 Thessalonians). In the 20th century the German scholar Erik Peterson developed the idea, and some still follow it: believers go up to welcome the Lord and return with him to earth. Michael Cosby (1994) argued that apantesis was not a technical term and that the main features of a formal civic welcome are missing from this passage. Robert Gundry (1996) replied that the parallels are closer than Cosby allows. Joseph Plevnik (1999) stressed that the passage is about the faithful being brought in to be with the Lord, not about the Lord being brought in. Compare Acts 28:15: "they came out to meet us at Appius' Market and at Three Taverns," and Matthew 25:6: "Go out and meet him!"
orig: εἰς ἀπάντησιν τοῦ κυρίου (eis apantesin tou kyriou)

p: Aer was the lower air between earth and heaven, the space where Ephesians places a hostile ruler.
b: In Greek thought aer was the lower, thicker air near the earth, below the bright upper sky. Ephesians 2:2 speaks of "the ruler of the domain of the air." The meeting takes place in the space between heaven and earth: the Lord comes down (4:16), the believers go up. Paul does not say where they go next; he says only that "we will be with the Lord always."

p: Paul ends with a call to use his words to comfort grieving believers: the passage was written to console.
b: Ancient letters of consolation, written to people in mourning, were a known kind of letter. Paul's passage is shaped for that use: it begins with grief (4:13) and ends with comfort (4:18), and it gives the readers words they can say to one another. In Orthodox worship 4:13-17 is the Epistle reading for funerals and for services for the departed. The passage was first written to console, not to set out a timetable of the end.

p: The same pair of words that Jesus uses in Acts 1:7, where he says the timing is not for the disciples to know.
b: Chronoi (times, spans of time) and kairoi (seasons, set moments) appear together in Acts 1:7: "Knowing the times or the seasons does not belong to you." Daniel says God "changes the periods and the appointed times" (Daniel 2:21). The church had asked, or Paul expected them to ask, when the Lord would come. He answers that they already know all they need: it will be sudden (5:2-3).

p: The prophets' day of the LORD's judgment, now the day when the Lord Jesus comes.
b: Amos warned those who longed for it: "Woe to you who long for the day of the LORD! / What will the day of the LORD be to you? / It is darkness, and not light" (Amos 5:18). Joel cried, "the day of the LORD is coming. / Yes, it is near" (Joel 2:1). Paul keeps the prophets' phrase, but "the Lord" in this letter is Jesus (4:15-17), so the day of the LORD has become the day of Jesus' coming. The same day brings ruin to some (5:3) and salvation to others (5:9).
r: Amos 5:18; Joel 2:1; Joel 2:31; Zephaniah 1:14-15; 1 Corinthians 1:8; 2 Thessalonians 2:2

a: the way a thief comes at night
p: The thief image goes back to Jesus' own sayings and recurs in Revelation.
b: Jesus said: "if the master of the house had known during which watch of the night the thief would come, he would have stayed awake" (Matthew 24:43; compare Luke 12:39). The risen Lord says in Revelation, "I will come like a thief" (Revelation 3:3) and "Look, I am coming like a thief!" (Revelation 16:15). The point is surprise, not secrecy: the coming will be unexpected for those not ready. Paul's use is probably the earliest written form of the saying.

p: The phrase may echo false prophets' "Peace, peace," or a Roman slogan of peace and security.
b: Two backgrounds are proposed. The prophets attacked those who promised calm before disaster, "saying, 'Peace, peace,' / when there is no peace" (Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 8:11; compare Ezekiel 13:10). Others hear Roman propaganda: the empire boasted of bringing peace (pax) and security (securitas). Jeffrey Weima (New Testament Studies, 2012) argued that Paul echoes this Roman claim, which he says was first proposed by Ernst Bammel in 1960. Joel White (New Testament Studies, 2013) answered that "peace" was central to imperial ideas but that the evidence for "peace and security" as a set Roman slogan in Paul's time is weak. The two backgrounds can overlap: false peace, whoever proclaims it.

p: A prophetic picture for sudden, unavoidable distress, used by Jesus of the end.
b: Isaiah describes the day of the LORD: "they will writhe like a woman giving birth" (Isaiah 13:8). Jesus calls the troubles before the end "only the start of the labor pains" (Matthew 24:8). Paul's picture stresses two things: the pains come suddenly, and once they begin there is no stopping them.

p: A Jewish idiom for people who belong to the light, known from the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Gospels.
b: "Sons of" in Hebrew idiom means "people marked by" or "belonging to." Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is the War Scroll (1QM), titled "The War of the Sons of Light Against the Sons of Darkness." Jesus uses the phrase too: "so that you will become sons of light" (John 12:36; compare Luke 16:8, "the children of light"). Paul tells Gentile converts that they belong to God's day, so the day of the Lord need not take them by surprise. The Plain keeps "sons," which in this idiom includes women.

p: Nepho means to be sober, the opposite of drunk; Paul pairs it with keeping awake.
b: Paul plays on night and day, sleep and waking, drunkenness and sobriety. Gregoreo ("stay awake") is the word Jesus uses: "So stay awake" (Matthew 24:42). Nepho ("be sober") means clear-headed. Romans 13:11-13 uses the same pictures: "It is already time for you to wake up out of sleep... The night is almost over. The day is close." Paul is not talking about literal sleep (see 5:10) but about living alert.

a: the breastplate of faith and love
p: Paul takes the armor that God wears in Isaiah 59:17 and puts it on believers.
b: In Isaiah God arms himself to rescue his people: "Righteousness he wore as his armor, / with salvation as a helmet on his head" (Isaiah 59:17). Paul puts the same pieces on the church, but changes the breastplate to faith and love and the helmet to the hope of salvation, so that the triad of 1:3 returns. Ephesians 6:14-17 later develops the full set: "righteousness put on as your breastplate" and "the helmet of salvation."

a: God did not appoint us to face anger
p: Readers who expect a rapture before the tribulation cite this verse; others take "anger" as the final judgment.
b: "Anger" here is the coming anger of 1:10, God's judgment on the day of the Lord (5:2-3). Pretribulational teachers read it as a promise that the church will be taken away before a coming time of God's anger on earth. Others answer that in this letter "anger" means the final judgment, from which believers are rescued at Christ's coming, and that believers are told to expect troubles (3:3). The verse's own contrast is between anger and salvation, not between earlier and later events.

p: The Greek editions differ on the small word for "for"; the English is the same either way.
b: NA28, Tyndale House, the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read hyper hemon, "on our behalf." The SBL text, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles read peri hemon, "for us, concerning us." Both say that his death was for our sake, so the Plain reads "for us" with either.

a: whether we stay awake or sleep
t: Awake or asleep: alive or dead
p: Here "asleep" means dead, though in 5:6 the same verb meant careless.
b: Paul uses katheudo, "sleep," for moral carelessness in 5:6-7, but here "whether we stay awake or sleep" must mean "alive or dead," since it picks up 4:13-17: whether we are among the living or the dead when he comes, we will live with him. The shift shows that the passage on the day of the Lord (5:1-11) and the passage on the dead (4:13-18) belong together.
orig: εἴτε γρηγορῶμεν εἴτε καθεύδωμεν (eite gregoromen eite katheudomen)

p: Proistamenoi means those who lead or care for others; Paul names no office.
b: Paul describes the church's leaders by what they do: they toil, they lead (proistamenoi), and they warn. The verb can mean "preside" or "protect, care for," as a patron cares for clients. The letter uses no titles such as elders or overseers. Some think these were the householders who hosted the church, like Jason (Acts 17:5-9). The young church needed to be told to respect people who had no title but did the work.

p: Ataktos meant out of rank, disorderly; in 2 Thessalonians 3 it is tied to those who will not work.
b: Ataktos was used of soldiers out of formation, and more broadly of anyone disorderly. The KJV has "unruly." Many recent Bibles say "idle," because 2 Thessalonians 3:6-11 uses the same word family of people who refused to work, and 4:11-12 has already urged work. The Plain keeps the wider sense "out of line" so that both meanings stay open.

p: Oligopsychos means "small-souled," discouraged; the KJV's "feebleminded" now misleads.
b: The Greek oligopsychos, literally "small of soul," means faint-hearted or discouraged. The KJV's "comfort the feebleminded" meant those weak in spirit, but today "feebleminded" suggests a mental disability, which the word does not mean. The verb paramytheomai means to speak comfort, as in 2:12.

t: How can anyone pray without a break?
p: Augustine said unceasing prayer is unceasing desire; the Orthodox Jesus Prayer grew in part from this verse.
b: Adialeiptos means without interruption; Paul used it of his own prayer and thanks (1:3; 2:13). Augustine, writing to Proba (Letter 130, AD 412), said that to "pray without ceasing" is to "desire without intermission" the life God gives, and he notes that "the brethren in Egypt are reported to have very frequent prayers, but these very brief" (chapters 9-10, in the New Advent translation). In the Eastern church the verse helped shape the Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me"), repeated through the day. The nineteenth-century Russian book The Way of a Pilgrim begins with a wanderer who hears this verse read in church and sets out to learn how to obey it.

a: Do not snuff out the Spirit
p: Sbennymi means to put out a fire; the Spirit is pictured as a flame that can be smothered.
b: The verb is used of quenching a fire or a lamp. The Spirit came at Pentecost as "Tongues that looked like fire" (Acts 2:3). In context (5:20-21), the Spirit is smothered when the church silences the gifts the Spirit gives, especially prophecy, out of suspicion or fear of disorder. Paul's answer is not to silence them but to test them.
orig: τὸ πνεῦμα μὴ σβέννυτε (to pneuma me sbennyte)

p: Believers spoke messages they believed came from God in the meetings; Paul says to weigh them, not scorn them.
b: In Paul's churches people prophesied in the gatherings: they spoke messages for the church that they believed God had given them (1 Corinthians 14:1-5). Some prophecy may have caused trouble in Thessalonica, perhaps about the day of the Lord (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:2). Paul's rule matches 1 Corinthians 14:29: "Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said."

p: Eidos means kind or form; the KJV's "appearance of evil" is often read as "anything that looks bad."
b: The KJV reads "Abstain from all appearance of evil," which many have taken to mean "avoid anything that might look wrong to others." The Greek eidos here means a kind or form: keep away from evil of every kind. In context the verse finishes the testing of prophecies (5:21): hold on to the good, keep away from every form of evil.
orig: ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδους πονηροῦ (apo pantos eidous ponerou)

p: A title Paul uses at the close of several letters.
b: Paul often closes with "the God of peace": "The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet, and soon" (Romans 16:20; compare Romans 15:33; Philippians 4:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:16 has "the Lord of peace"). In a letter that warns against a false "Peace and safety" (5:3) and asks the church to "Keep the peace" (5:13), Paul names the God who alone gives real peace.

a: your spirit and soul and body
t: Spirit, soul and body: three parts or one person?
p: Some read three parts of a human being; most churches read a way of saying "all of you."
b: Paul lists "spirit and soul and body" together here. Some Christians (trichotomists) take it as proof that a human being has three parts. Irenaeus, in the second century, quoted it and said "the perfect man consists in the commingling and the union of the soul receiving the spirit of the Father, and the admixture of that fleshly nature" (Against Heresies, book 5, chapter 6). Others (dichotomists) hold that a person is body and soul, and that Paul piles up words to say "every part of you," as in "with all your heart, with all your being, with all your mind and with all your strength" (Mark 12:30). The Reformed theologian Louis Berkhof wrote that this verse and Hebrews 4:12 "do not prove the point" of three parts, and that Paul may be naming aspects of the one person (Manual of Christian Doctrine). The Catholic Catechism (367) cites this verse and says, "The Church teaches that this distinction does not introduce a duality into the soul."
orig: ὑμῶν τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὸ σῶμα (hymon to pneuma kai he psyche kai to soma)

p: A greeting kiss among believers, later part of Christian worship.
b: Paul ends four letters with a call to greet with a "holy kiss" (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 2 Corinthians 13:12; here), and 1 Peter 5:14 has a "kiss of love." In the ancient world a kiss was a greeting among family and close friends; among believers it marked the new family. By the mid-second century it was part of worship: Justin Martyr wrote, "Having ended the prayers, we salute one another with a kiss" (First Apology 65). Many churches keep it as the "sign of peace."

a: I bind you with an oath
p: Paul's oath makes sure the letter is read aloud to the whole church, perhaps to several house churches.
b: Paul switches to "I" and uses a strong verb, enorkizo, "put under oath." Letters were read aloud when the church gathered. The oath may mean the church met in several houses and Paul wanted every group to hear it, or that he feared some would keep it from others. It is the first sign of the practice that turned Paul's letters into texts read in worship (compare Colossians 4:16), the first step toward their place in the New Testament.
orig: ἐνορκίζω ὑμᾶς τὸν κύριον (enorkizo hymas ton kyrion)
